title: Germany invades Poland
subtitle: The invasion and the battle for time
author: R.G. Cruise
location: Poland and the Free City of Danzig
summary: Germany’s overwhelming advantages met effective resistance at bridges, fortified positions and village railway lines. The opening campaign turned on how quickly each army could move, recover and respond.
sourceMethod: The study compares German operational reporting with Polish military scholarship, museum accounts and contemporary diplomatic documents. Kennedy’s 1956 U.S. Army study is used for command assignments and identified operational reports, not its discredited cavalry-charge story or claims that Polish aviation was eliminated in the opening days. Reported advances describe leading units, not verified daily control boundaries. Disputed loss totals and Wieluń raid timings are qualified. Source notes identify the evidence and its limits.

sections.label: Mokra and the price of delay
The invasion becomes a European war

body:
The attempt to seize the Vistula bridges at Tczew before dawn on 1 September 1939 reveals the operational problem at the beginning of Germany’s invasion. Aircraft attacked the demolition installations while a railway operation sought to bring troops to the crossings before the Polish defenders could destroy them. German success required synchronisation: firepower and surprise had to preserve the infrastructure needed by the advancing army. Polish personnel frustrated the seizure, and the bridges were demolished during the morning. This opening failure illustrates the distinction that governs the campaign: Germany possessed overwhelming advantages, but still had to convert them into movement through defended terrain. The Tczew air attack is usually placed at approximately 4:34 a.m., before the better-known bombardment of Westerplatte. Its significance extends beyond precedence in the chronology. German commanders sought to reach crossings and road junctions before Polish formations could withdraw or concentrate; Polish commanders needed time to assemble reserves and establish a coherent defence. The bridges became part of that unequal contest over operational tempo—the rate at which an army could sustain effective action. A successful demolition could interrupt one axis of advance even as a breakthrough elsewhere compromised the defender’s wider position. [1] [2] The agreement signed in Moscow on 23 August had made the strategic setting more dangerous for Poland. Germany could attack without expecting Soviet intervention to preserve Polish independence, while the secret protocol anticipated territorial rearrangements at Poland’s expense. Yet the bargain was neither a completed partition nor a joint timetable for the operations of 1 September. The Red Army had not invaded. Polish government, armies and population still occupied a country whose defeat remained a military objective, not an accomplished fact. This study concentrates on the opening attack, then follows selected consequences through the Bzura fighting and Warsaw’s resistance. Those later developments are dated explicitly; the separate Soviet invasion is examined in the following study. [3]

The order and the pretext

By the time German troops crossed the frontier, the machinery of aggression had been running for months. The army’s plan, Fall Weiss, aimed to destroy Poland’s armed forces before they could escape the converging German offensives. The disputes over Danzig and transit across the Polish Corridor provided the diplomatic setting, but the operational design reached far beyond a border adjustment. The destruction of Czechoslovakia earlier in the year had enlarged Germany’s southern approaches into Poland, giving military planners another direction from which to threaten the Polish rear. Their task was to exploit that geography quickly enough to prevent an effective defence from taking shape. [4] There had already been a false start. Hitler intended the offensive to begin on 26 August, then postponed it after developments including the formal Anglo-Polish alliance signed on the 25th. A German commando detachment failed to receive the cancellation in time and attacked the railway route near the Jabłonków Pass. Polish resistance defeated the attempt to secure the tunnel and station for the coming army. The episode belongs to the transition between diplomacy and war, and it exposes the practical character of the preparations: the seizure of infrastructure was important enough to put small advance parties across the frontier before the main formations arrived. [5] On 31 August, Hitler issued Directive No. 1 for the Conduct of the War. It specified the next day and 4:45 a.m. for the attack, including the operation against the Tczew bridges. Its opening language blamed an allegedly intolerable situation on Germany’s eastern frontier, but the document itself recorded a decision for force made in advance. The same directive restrained German action in the west, where Hitler wanted Britain and France to bear responsibility for widening the conflict. He was ordering a war against Poland while trying to control how other powers would enter it. [6] The regime’s public explanation inverted the responsibility disclosed by its own orders. SS personnel staged the Gleiwitz radio-station incident on 31 August as evidence of supposed Polish aggression, while press instructions presented German action as defensive and discouraged the term war. These measures sought to shape the interpretation of an offensive whose preparations were already complete. Their place in the chronology is decisive: the staged provocations served the policy of aggression, rather than furnishing an unforeseen reason to undertake it. [7]

Inside the diplomatic record

Proposals the ambassador never received

On the afternoon of 1 September, Polish ambassador Józef Lipski told the American chargé in Berlin that he had not even been furnished with the German proposals supposedly offered as a basis for negotiation. This was Lipski’s account, recorded by the American diplomat, and it undercuts the image of a straightforward settlement rejected after normal discussions. The army was already advancing while diplomats were still documenting how the appearance of negotiation had been maintained.

[8]

Two armies, two different problems

Germany’s advantage was considerable, although campaign totals can conceal the conditions under which particular engagements were fought. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives approximately 1.5 million German troops, around sixty divisions and more than two thousand tanks for the invading force. A Polish museum estimate places the forces Poland fielded during September at about 900,000. These are broad campaign measures, not synchronised headcounts of men in their battle positions at dawn on the first day. Polish mobilisation and concentration remained incomplete. Germany could choose the places where its strongest forces would strike; Poland was still assembling parts of the army with which it had to resist them. [9] [10] The organisation of German strength helps explain its effect. Armoured and motorised formations concentrated mobility, artillery, engineering and communications for operational tasks, with Luftwaffe support. Much of the army nevertheless advanced as ordinary infantry. The different rates of movement created a division of labour: mobile formations threatened crossings and communications, while following troops engaged bypassed Polish forces and secured routes. This arrangement could sustain a succession of crises for the defender, provided the advancing columns retained supply and contact with the forces behind them. Its effectiveness depended on the coordination of arms and echelons, rather than on tanks considered in isolation. [4] [11] Polish infantry, artillery and anti-tank weapons were capable of defeating German attacks, and cavalry formations generally used horses for movement while fighting dismounted with machine guns, anti-tank rifles and 37 mm guns. The operational difficulty lay in concentrating sufficient force, maintaining contact between formations and withdrawing before routes were cut. Local firepower could impose substantial losses without giving a defender the mobility required to respond to a threat developing elsewhere. Polish tactical competence consequently remained compatible with a steadily worsening theatre-wide position. Understanding that relationship avoids treating defeat as evidence that resistance was intrinsically ineffective. [12] The air comparison was harsher. The RAF Museum sets roughly three hundred mostly obsolete Polish aircraft against more than thirteen hundred German fighters and bombers. Polish squadrons had dispersed to field airfields before the attack, so the familiar story that the Luftwaffe destroyed them on the ground at the outset is false. Their survival allowed real resistance, but dispersal could not cancel the disparity in numbers, performance and capacity to sustain operations. Germany could commit aircraft against the fighting front, transport system and targets farther inside Poland while the smaller Polish force faced difficult choices about where to expend its strength. [13] Marshal Edward Rydz-Śmigły’s armies also faced a geographical problem for which there was no painless answer. A shorter position deeper in the country would have surrendered important industrial districts, population centres and access to the sea before a serious battle. A defence near the frontier committed troops to a broad arc threatened from the west, East Prussia and the south. The Polish plan tried to defend essential territory while preserving the possibility of withdrawal and continued resistance. Its success depended on time, communications and assistance from abroad—the very conditions the German offensive was intended to disrupt. [4]

Reading the offensive

Two German army groups directed the attack. **Army Group North**, under Fedor von Bock, brought together Third Army in East Prussia and Fourth Army in Pomerania. Georg von Küchler’s Third Army faced the Polish northern approaches, including the fortified position at Mława on the route towards Warsaw. Günther von Kluge’s Fourth Army attacked across the Corridor, seeking to cut off Polish formations and establish land communications with East Prussia. Within Fourth Army, Heinz Guderian’s XIX Corps supplied a powerful mobile striking force. The northern operation thus combined a drive into Poland with the practical need to connect two German concentration areas separated by Polish territory. [4] **Army Group South**, under Gerd von Rundstedt, contained the heavier concentration. Johannes Blaskowitz’s Eighth Army advanced towards Łódź and covered the northern flank of Walther von Reichenau’s Tenth Army, whose armoured concentration drove from Silesia towards the interior and Warsaw. Wilhelm List’s Fourteenth Army operated through the southern approaches towards Kraków and farther east. These assignments formed a connected operational design: the flanking armies protected the principal advance while threatening Polish forces that might otherwise turn against it. The movement towards Warsaw therefore depended on operations extending well beyond the route of the leading armour. [4] The Polish commands were arranged around the territory they had to defend. Army Pomorze under Władysław Bortnowski covered the Corridor; Army Modlin under Emil Krukowicz-Przedrzymirski faced the threat from East Prussia. Farther west and south stood Tadeusz Kutrzeba’s Army Poznań, Juliusz Rómmel’s Army Łódź and Antoni Szylling’s Army Kraków. Army Karpaty covered the southeastern approaches, the Narew Operational Group the northeast, and Army Prusy formed the principal strategic reserve. Their names are useful geographical guides, but the spaces between these forces were as consequential as their individual positions. Germany’s converging advances threatened to separate them, close their withdrawal routes and commit the reserves before those reserves were fully assembled. [4]

Slovakia made the southern threat more extensive. Its German-dependent government permitted the use of Slovak territory and committed forces of its own. Two Slovak divisions took part from 1 September, attacking towards places including Bukowina Tatrzańska, Krynica and Muszyna. Their contribution was much smaller than Germany’s, but it widened the area Polish commanders had to watch and defend. The political destruction of Czechoslovakia had become an immediate military disadvantage for Poland: the southern frontier now offered an attacker opportunities that had not existed in the same form a year earlier. [14]

Crossings and strongpoints

The operation at Tczew demonstrates why the rivers on an atlas need to be read as military obstacles. Aircraft could fly over the Vistula; the vehicles and supply columns required a crossing. German bombing sought to interfere with the demolition system, while the railway approach attempted to deliver a force before the defenders could destroy the bridges. Polish railway workers at Szymankowo helped raise the alarm and frustrate the surprise. Enough of the defensive arrangements survived for the bridges to be demolished. The German operation had failed in its immediate purpose even though aircraft and troops had reached their objectives. [1] [2] Farther north, the battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on Westerplatte shortly before five in the morning. The Polish Military Transit Depot lay within the Free City of Danzig, and its defenders faced a concentration of firepower that appeared disproportionate to the small garrison. Major Henryk Sucharski commanded a force of a little over two hundred. The initial German assaults nevertheless failed, and the position remained in Polish hands at the end of the day. It would continue resisting until 7 September. Prepared defences and disciplined fire gave a small force an ability to survive that could not be inferred simply by counting men or comparing the size of their weapons. [15] [11] Mława presented a larger obstacle. Here the principal fortified position was defended by the Polish 20th Infantry Division within Army Modlin. Küchler’s Third Army encountered concrete defensive works, artillery and anti-tank fire after making progress earlier in the day. German infantry attacks met strong resistance; armour brought forward to break the position also failed to secure the expected result. The fighting continued on 2 September, while German forces sought opportunities to the east. The eventual threat to the defenders developed through outflanking and the deterioration of the wider position, rather than a simple repetition of the first frontal assault until Polish resistance disappeared. [16]

Mokra and the price of delay

At Mokra, northwest of Częstochowa, Colonel Julian Filipowicz’s Wołyńska Cavalry Brigade occupied ground between Army Łódź and Army Kraków. Its mission was to delay the enemy and maintain contact with neighbouring formations while the larger Polish deployment took shape. This was a professional assignment to a mobile covering force, and the terrain offered ways to carry it out. Woods restricted movement, the villages channelled approaches, and a railway embankment running along the eastern side of the position formed an obstacle to tanks. The brigade’s ability to use those features helped turn an apparent mismatch into a day of repeated German frustration. [17] The opposing 4th Panzer Division was a much stronger formation, with tanks, motorised infantry, artillery, engineers and supporting troops. Military historian Juliusz S. Tym gives its strength as 357 tanks; that is a divisional figure, not a claim that all those vehicles attacked the same Polish position simultaneously. The German advantage was therefore both substantial and more complicated than the image of a solid mass of tanks advancing against horsemen. Effective armour needed accompanying infantry and supporting fire. At several points the Polish defence exploited the vulnerability of tanks that had moved beyond adequate support, while German efforts became more coordinated as the day continued. [17] The Polish cavalry fought largely dismounted. Its anti-tank guns and artillery could engage the relatively lightly protected German vehicles, while the armoured train Śmiały added mobile firepower along the railway. Success required more than possessing the weapons: crews had to remain in action under bombardment, ammunition had to reach the guns, and threatened parts of the position needed support before they were overwhelmed. The terrain narrowed the choices available to attackers, allowing defenders to concentrate fire on approaches and openings. German assaults repeatedly entered dangerous ground without obtaining the decisive passage they needed. The brigade bought time through the use of weapons, terrain and local command. [12] The delay imposed at Mokra consumed Polish strength as well as German time. Repeated attacks and bombardment required adjustments and eventual withdrawal, but retaining enough cohesion to move was itself part of a covering force’s task. The brigade’s achievement should be assessed against that assignment. It disrupted the immediate advance without acquiring the means to determine what happened on neighbouring sectors. German movement elsewhere could still threaten the routes behind the position. The episode thus demonstrates both the military value of a successful delaying action and the conditions that limited its effect on the campaign. [17] [12]

Reading a battlefield total

A disabled tank is not always a destroyed tank

Published loss figures for Mokra vary, and a total of vehicles hit or temporarily disabled should not be presented as a count of permanent write-offs. Recovery and repair could return a tank to service. The securely established result is more useful here: the Polish brigade defeated repeated attempts at an immediate breakthrough. This account avoids turning disputed vehicle totals into an exact scoreboard.

[12] [17]
The cavalry myth derived in part from a different engagement at Krojanty, where Polish horsemen charged infantry before coming under fire from armoured vehicles. Its later transformation into an attack on tanks with sabres supplied propaganda with a supposed explanation of national backwardness. That interpretation obscured the actual military question. At Mokra, cavalrymen using anti-tank weapons and favourable terrain checked an armoured formation; elsewhere, German operational mobility threatened the wider defensive system. Explaining the campaign requires attention to those relationships rather than an inference about the competence of an entire army drawn from a distorted anecdote. [10]

Measuring the advance

The opening advance varied sharply by formation and sector. Robert M. Kennedy’s U.S. Army reconstruction reports forward elements of Army Group South three to four miles inside Poland by 6 a.m., with some units reaching fifteen miles by late afternoon—approximately five to six kilometres and twenty-four kilometres respectively. These figures describe selected leading elements. They provide evidence of rapid penetration without measuring an army-wide average or the depth of securely occupied territory. Read alongside the checks at Mława and Mokra, they reveal an offensive developing through uneven progress, in which movement on one axis could alter the value of resistance on another. [11] The limits of that progress appeared in the north on **2 September**, when, according to Kennedy’s reconstruction, armoured elements of XIX Corps outran their petrol and ammunition after crossing the Brda. Supply columns had to fight through withdrawing Polish troops to reach them. The interruption was temporary, but it reveals a consequential vulnerability within a successful advance: the route connecting the spearhead to its supplies still contained hostile forces. Operational reach consequently exceeded the security of the communications on which further movement depended. [11] By 3 September, the German Third and Fourth Armies had established contact across the Corridor, gravely worsening Army Pomorze’s position. In the south, the advance reached Kraków on 6 September, and the 4th Panzer Division reached Warsaw’s outskirts on the 8th. These milestones reveal a formidable capacity to exploit the opening battles, but arrival outside the capital did not mean possession of it. Warsaw continued to resist until 28 September. The contrast in dates measures the difference between a successful operational approach and the reduction of a defended city; it should not be collapsed into a claim that Poland had been defeated in a week. [11] [9] Army Poznań, comparatively little engaged at the outset, retained forces with which Kutrzeba could strike the exposed northern flank of the German Eighth Army. On **9 September**, his counteroffensive across the Bzura began around Łęczyca and Piątek; troops of Army Pomorze joined the fighting. Its initial success forced Germany to turn forces against a threat behind the advance towards Warsaw. The attack demonstrated that Polish commanders could identify and exploit an operational opportunity even after the frontier defence had broken down. [18] The opportunity narrowed as the surrounding situation changed. The retreat of Army Łódź undermined the prospect of a combined effort, while German redeployment threatened the Polish attackers with encirclement. Renewed fighting around Łowicz was followed by attempts to cross the Bzura and reach the Kampinos Forest. German forces concentrated against the crossing routes, and many Polish formations were destroyed or captured, although some troops reached Warsaw and Modlin. The battle’s significance lies in both results: it disrupted Germany’s timetable, yet the attacker possessed sufficient reserves and mobility to turn disruption into another encirclement. [18] Warsaw presented a different problem. German armour reached its outskirts on **8 September**, but early attempts to take the city failed. Urban defences deprived mobile formations of some of the freedom they had enjoyed on open roads, while retreating Polish units reinforced the capital. Its eventual capitulation on **28 September** followed a siege in which bombardment and damage to essential services made the position of civilians increasingly desperate. The three weeks between arrival and surrender were consequential: Germany could reach the capital quickly without being able to compel its immediate submission. Warsaw’s defence also maintained a visible centre of resistance while much of the field army was being forced into retreat or encirclement. [11] [9] The term *Blitzkrieg*, or lightning war, can describe the campaign’s striking mobility only if it leaves room for the failures that shaped the actual fighting. Kennedy’s operational account records interruptions in reconnaissance, coordination and supply, while Juliusz S. Tym’s study of Mokra shows how unsupported armour could be checked. German superiority lay partly in the capacity to recover from such failures by concentrating forces and restoring momentum. Poland had fewer means to compensate when a local reverse threatened the cohesion of adjacent armies. The unequal capacity to absorb disruption is more explanatory than an image of uninterrupted technical mastery. [11] [17]

The war beyond the front

The destruction of transport and communications affected soldiers and civilians together. Air attack could delay reserves, interrupt a railway movement or make a road unsafe, while people fleeing the fighting entered the same transport network on which the army depended. To describe this only as interdiction would leave out the experience of those beneath the aircraft. At Wieluń, German bombing struck the town and its hospital on the first morning. An investigation by Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance found that no Polish military units were present in the town on the eve of the invasion or on 1 September. The attack killed civilians, including hospital patients and personnel, far from any meaningful contest between equivalent military forces. [19] The exact timing of the first raid remains disputed, as does the complete number of victims. The investigation could document deaths but could not establish a final toll, and it challenged some higher figures repeated in commemorative accounts. The uncertainty over the clock and the count leaves the central findings intact: civilians were killed, patients and personnel died, and a hospital was struck in a town without the military units sometimes invoked to explain the raid. For the people beneath the bombs, the war arrived without the protection that even an inadequate defensive position might have offered. [19] [20] Violence also accompanied the ground forces. In the Parzymiechy area, close to the fighting south of Wieluń, Polish infantry resisted German troops through the first day before withdrawing towards Działoszyn. Paweł Żołądek’s research for the Institute of National Remembrance, based principally on witness testimony, describes German soldiers searching houses, seizing civilians and killing people during the occupation of the villages. Such actions belong inside the history of the advance. Treating the campaign only as a contest of arrows and formations can make civilians disappear at the very moment when the arrival of those formations transformed their lives. [21] German security forces also pursued political objectives behind the advancing armies. Einsatzgruppen—mobile security-police and Security Service formations—and other SS and police units participated in the destruction of potential Polish leadership. [22] Arrests and killings of officials, clergy and educated professionals made conquest an attack on the institutions through which society might organise resistance. The occupation system examined in the October study would develop these policies further, but organised persecution was already part of the invasion’s consequences. [23] Military disadvantage and civilian exposure arose within the same invasion but require different explanations. Polish units could exploit terrain, weapons and command to impose costs on the attacker, even under unfavourable conditions. Patients in a hospital and families seized after the fighting had no comparable capacity to influence events. Operational history therefore needs to follow the movement of formations into the relationships of power their arrival created. The treatment of inhabitants was part of how conquest unfolded, with identifiable institutions and perpetrators whose conduct cannot be explained simply as an incidental consequence of rapid movement.

The invasion becomes a European war

Britain and France had not declared war when the first day ended. Their governments demanded that Germany stop its attack and withdraw, while still testing whether diplomacy could prevent a wider conflict. The distinction mattered in Poland, where each interval of discussion was also an interval of German advance. The parliamentary record of 1 September shows the British government presenting withdrawal as the condition that could avert the consequences of its commitment to Poland. [24] Italy then proposed a conference involving the European powers. Reporting to Parliament on the evening of **2 September**, Chamberlain said that Britain could not take part while Poland remained under invasion and bombardment: German withdrawal would have to precede negotiations. The proposal therefore turned on a material question, not simply a willingness to talk. A conference held under continuing occupation might preserve Germany’s gains while postponing the moment when its opponents acted. Consultation with France also affected the timing of the British ultimatum. [25] On **3 September**, the British demand for an assurance of withdrawal expired at eleven in the morning. Chamberlain told the Commons that Britain was at war with Germany; France entered the war later that day. These were decisions for belligerency, with consequences extending far beyond a diplomatic protest. They nevertheless did not provide the immediate offensive relief on which Polish hopes depended. The French advance in the Saar was limited, while the British Expeditionary Force began arriving in France on **9 September**. The Allies were organising for a sustained war, with defensive preparations and economic pressure playing central roles. Poland was fighting an emergency measured in days. [26] [9] [27] The absence of effective relief reflected Allied mobilisation, deployment and assumptions about the kind of war they would fight. These constraints require examination because a major offensive could not be produced by declaration alone. They nevertheless left a decisive mismatch between the timescale of Allied preparation and the Polish emergency. Britain and France accepted belligerency while failing to divert sufficient German strength soon enough to preserve Poland’s initial defensive position. The distinction explains the outcome without turning either diplomatic commitment or military constraint into a complete account of Allied responsibility. [27] The United States made a different set of decisions. Roosevelt proclaimed neutrality on **5 September**, imposing the duties of a non-belligerent state without requiring Americans to suppress their opinions or sympathies. On **21 September**, he asked Congress to repeal the arms-embargo provisions of the neutrality legislation. His proposal sought to change the rules governing trade with belligerents while keeping the United States out of the war; it was not an announcement of American military intervention, nor had the proposed repeal yet become law. American diplomacy, public sympathy and the supply question belonged to the international response, but none was equivalent to an army relieving Poland. [28] [29] Hungary’s conduct also resists a simple division between Germany’s friends and Poland’s friends. Its government pursued cooperation with Germany and had benefited from territorial revision, yet refused participation in the attack on Poland and denied the requested transit of German forces against it. It subsequently enabled Polish escape routes through Hungary towards the forces being assembled abroad. These decisions differed sharply from Slovakia’s participation in the invasion. Neighbouring governments operated under German pressure, but their responses were not identical, and those differences materially affected Polish opportunities for survival and continued resistance. [30] By the end of 1 September, the failed seizure at Tczew and the resistance at Westerplatte, Mława and Mokra stood alongside dangerous German penetrations elsewhere. Polish commanders’ central difficulty was to connect these local achievements into a sustainable defence while their opponents generated new threats along several axes. German superiority operated through that cumulative pressure, and Allied belligerency did not immediately remove it. The [Soviet invasion of 17 September](/articles/soviet-invasion-poland-1939-09-17) would then close much of the remaining eastern space through which military units, officials and refugees were still attempting to move.
